notes.b: A warm house loses heat to the cold outside all the time. Insulation does not make heat; it slows the escape of heat, so less fuel is needed to keep the house warm.
points: Heat leaves a house in four ways: by conduction through solid parts such as walls and glass, by convection (warm air rising and leaking out), by radiation (heat given off as rays), and by air leakage through gaps. Insulation reduces these losses, so less fuel is needed.

Insulating materials are poor conductors of heat. Still air is a very poor conductor, so poor conductors such as still air, polystyrene, fibreglass, mineral wool, sheep's wool, cellulose and foam trap air in small pockets, which reduces heat transfer by conduction.

Fibre and foam insulation holds air in small cells that are too small for convection currents to form. Because the air cannot circulate, it cannot carry heat by convection, which is why a big open gap is not insulation.
Reflective foil and low-emissivity (low-E) coatings (thin coatings that give off little heat) reflect radiant heat back, so they reduce heat loss by radiation.
Draught proofing stops heat leaving in moving air, because it seals the gaps around doors, windows and floorboards where air leaks.
Insulation also keeps a house cool in hot weather, because it slows heat moving in as well as out.
notes.tip: If asked for the underlying principle, say that insulating materials are poor conductors and that the still air trapped in them does the work. Then give an example such as a cavity wall, double glazing or a lagging jacket. Do not say insulation keeps the cold out or generates heat.

notes.b: Warm air rises, so the roof is a main route of heat loss. Insulating the attic is the cheapest and most effective place to start.
points: Fibre blanket or quilt: strips of mineral or glass fibre, or wool, are laid between and over the ceiling joists (the beams that carry the ceiling).
Loose fill: pellets of polystyrene or vermiculite are poured between the joists.
Sprayed or foam insulation: foam is applied between the roof rafters (the sloping beams that hold the roof), where it expands and sets into a solid layer.
Blown fibre: cellulose or mineral fibre is blown into the roof space to cover it evenly.
Rigid boards are fitted between the rafters in a converted attic, where the roof space is used as a room.
Once the attic floor is insulated, the attic becomes colder, so lag the cold water tank and attic pipes to stop them freezing. Insulate and draught-proof the hatch, and keep the eaves ventilated.
Diagram: cross-section of a roof showing the joists, the ceiling below and an insulation layer laid between and over the joists, with the roof space above.
notes.tip: Name a material and say where it goes, for example mineral fibre blanket laid between the joists. Writing only 'insulate the attic' earns few marks.

notes.b: Walls are a large surface through which heat escapes. The method depends on whether the wall has a cavity (a gap between two layers of wall) or is solid.
points: Cavity wall insulation: a cavity wall has an outer and an inner leaf (layer) with a gap between them. The cavity is filled with polystyrene beads, foam or mineral wool blown in through small holes, and even an unfilled cavity holds some still air.
Internal dry lining: insulated plasterboard is fixed to the inside face of the wall, which adds insulation on the room side. It reduces room size and takes time to fit, but needs no scaffolding.

External insulation: boards of polystyrene or mineral wool are fixed to the outside of the wall and finished with reinforced, waterproof render. This keeps the wall itself warm and avoids thermal bridges (cold spots where heat escapes), but needs planning checks.
Solid walls have no cavity, so they can only be insulated from the inside (dry lining) or the outside (external insulation).
Diagram: cross-section of a cavity wall showing the outer leaf, the insulation in the cavity, the inner leaf and an internal dry lining.
notes.tip: When asked to recommend a method for walls, give its name, how it is fitted and the principle behind it (the insulation traps still air, which is a poor conductor).

notes.h: Insulating floors, windows, doors and pipes
notes.b: Heat also escapes through floors, glass, gaps around doors and bare pipes. Each has its own simple method.
points: Floors: seal the gaps between floorboards, add insulation between the joists on suspended floors, and lay a carpet with underlay. Rigid insulation goes under a new concrete floor. All of these reduce heat loss through the floor.

Double glazing: two panes are separated by a sealed gap of air or argon (a gas used instead of air in some units). The trapped gas is a poor conductor and cannot circulate, so conduction and convection across the gap are reduced.
Triple glazing adds a third pane and a second sealed gap for further insulation.
Low-E glazing: a thin coating on the pane reflects radiant heat back into the room.
Secondary glazing (an extra window fitted inside the existing one), heavy lined curtains and blinds close to the glass, and shutters trap a layer of still air against cold glass.

Doors and gaps: draught excluders, brush strips on doors, a letterbox flap, keyhole covers and sealing strips around windows and floorboards stop air leaking in and out. A porch adds a buffer of still air.
Lagging: an insulating jacket or factory-fitted foam on the hot-water cylinder and sleeves on exposed pipes save heat and help prevent pipes freezing.
Insulation reduces condensation, because warm inner surfaces stay above the temperature at which moisture condenses. However, an airtight, well-insulated house needs controlled ventilation.
notes.tip: Name a method for each area asked. For windows give double or triple glazing, low-E or lined curtains, with the principle that sealed trapped air or gas reduces conduction and convection. For floors, doors and pipes give fill gaps and carpet with underlay, draught excluders and lagging.

notes.b: Examiners often ask for the benefits of insulation. Each one follows from less heat escaping.
points: Lower heating bills, because less heat escapes and the heating runs for shorter periods.
Comfort: a steadier indoor temperature with no cold surfaces and fewer draughts.
Less noise, because insulation absorbs sound from outside and between rooms.
Less fuel burned, so lower carbon dioxide emissions and less use of fossil fuel, which makes a more sustainable house.
Less condensation and damp, because inner wall and window surfaces stay warm. This means healthier air and less mould.

A better Building Energy Rating (BER), which rates a dwelling's energy performance on a scale from A (most efficient) to G (least efficient) and is run by SEAI. A better BER can also raise the value of the property.
SEAI grants may help with the cost of insulating.
notes.tip: Give three or four advantages and attach a reason to each, for example lower bills because the heating runs for shorter periods.

notes.h: Practical context: evaluating insulation in your own home
notes.b: You may be asked to assess the insulation in your own home and suggest improvements. The method is to inspect, rank the problems and justify each recommendation.
points: Inspect the attic for the depth and coverage of insulation. Check whether joists are left uncovered and whether the tank and pipes are lagged.
Check doors and windows for draughts by feeling for cold air around the frames on a windy day, and note the type of glazing.
Find out the wall type (cavity or solid) and check whether the hot-water cylinder has a jacket.
Note cold rooms, cold surfaces and any signs of condensation or damp.
Recommend improvements in order of cost and effect: draught proofing and attic insulation first, then a cylinder jacket and lined curtains, then wall insulation and glazing.
Justify each recommendation by the heat it saves and its cost, and mention SEAI grants and the BER.
notes.tip: Recommend a method for each area asked, such as the attic, walls and windows. Give its name, a description and the principle each time.

keyTerms.definition: A material or method that reduces the transfer of heat through the fabric of a building.
Window glass with a thin coating that reflects radiant heat back into the room while letting light through.
Two panes of glass separated by a sealed gap of air or argon, which reduces heat loss through a window.
Sealing the gaps around doors, windows and floors to stop air leaking in and out of a room.
Insulating material placed in the gap between the two leaves of a cavity wall.
Insulated plasterboard fixed to the inside face of a wall to add insulation on the room side.
An insulating jacket or sleeve placed around a hot-water cylinder or pipe to reduce heat loss.
Insulating pellets, such as polystyrene or vermiculite, poured between the joists of an attic floor.
Strips of mineral or glass fibre laid between ceiling joists or rafters to trap air and reduce heat loss.
A rating from A (best) to G (worst) that shows how much energy a dwelling needs to heat and run.

factCards.term: Four methods of insulating a home
factCards.definition: Attic insulation, cavity wall insulation, double or triple glazing, and floor insulation with carpet and underlay.

factCards.term: Three advantages of a well-insulated home
factCards.definition: Lower fuel bills, a steadier indoor temperature, and less carbon dioxide released from burning fuel.

factCards.term: Five poor conductors used in insulation
factCards.definition: Trapped air, polystyrene, fibreglass, wool and cellulose.

factCards.term: Gas used between the panes of some double glazing
factCards.definition: Argon, which conducts heat less well than air.

factCards.term: Three ways to stop draughts at windows and doors
factCards.definition: Draught excluders, sealing strips around frames, and lined curtains.

factCards.term: Two wall insulation methods for a solid wall
factCards.definition: Internal dry lining and external insulation covered with reinforced render.

factCards.term: Two effects of a low-E coating on a window
factCards.definition: It reflects radiant heat back into the room and lets visible light pass through.

questions.prompt: Identify three benefits to a household of fitting cavity wall insulation to its house.
questions.model: Any three of: less heat lost through the walls, so lower fuel bills (2 marks); a steadier temperature in rooms with fewer cold walls, so more comfort (2 marks); less fuel burned, so lower carbon dioxide emissions (2 marks). Also accepted: less noise from outside and between rooms; less condensation on inner wall surfaces.

questions.prompt: Explain the underlying principle by which insulation reduces heat loss from a home. Describe three methods of insulating different parts of a home, and state the area each method protects.
questions.model: Principle: insulating materials are poor conductors of heat and trap still air in small spaces, which slows heat transfer by conduction and limits convection. Reflective coatings reduce heat loss by radiation, and draught proofing reduces air leakage. Method 1, attic: fibre blanket, loose fill, sprayed foam or blown fibre laid in or above the roof space to protect the ceiling and roof. Method 2, walls: cavity wall insulation of beads, foam or mineral wool in a cavity, or internal dry lining or external insulation with render for solid walls. Method 3, windows: double or triple glazing with a sealed air or argon gap and low-E coating, combined with lined curtains. Each method reduces the heat escaping through the area it covers, so less fuel is needed to keep the house warm.
